b:
I guess I didn't make myself clear.

As of now, I do believe that homosexuality is sinful according to God's laws. And I believe it is very important that God's people obey God's laws. However, it is not important that I go around telling the people around me how wrong they are. Unfortunately, many people have made it their business to tell gay people how wrong they are by saying very hateful things. That ignorant behavior has become so common that if I simply mention that I believe homosexuality is sinful, I may (almost always) get put in the same box with all those hateful people. In addition to that, my friend does not consider himself one of God's people, so for me to tell him that he's not obeying God's laws would mean nothing to him except that he might think I'm looking down on him. So what I said was not merely an effort to avoid saying how I feel. I honestly said exactly what I think. There are lots of things that matter. My stance on this issue is one of those things that matters, but there are more important things to talk about.

I did not downplay it. Prior to this, I had spent about an hour consoling him about his dad (who had said some very hateful things about his sexuality) and ensuring him that I love him even if other people are hateful.

> That's why they asked the question, and, as you said, after numerous attempts to avoid the question, you still avoided answering it honestly. Why would you continually make efforts to avoid that question? Are you that insecure about where you stand?

I did not make attempts to skirt the question. I made attempts to avoid the conversation (about whether or not homosexuality is sinful), because Christians already say far too much on the subject. But since he asked, I did answer honestly. I told him exactly what I think. And I am very secure about where I stand. I have approached the issue very torn and open-minded, and, after much deliberation and prayer, I conclusively gathered that homosexuality is sinful. But I also concluded that we (Christians) should be focusing on all the positive effects of a relationship with God - not all the things that the people around us are doing wrong.

I try to focus on the positive things in life. And I believe that, by doing that, the negative will have no room to grow.

That is not asinine.

I was not dishonest. Everything I said is exactly what I think and how I feel. You should know that in response he thanked me for my honesty and open-mindedness.

> So your stance is important, just not important enough to talk about when your friend asks?

Yes, exactly. My friend wanted to know if I was going to one day reveal that I had secretly hated him for being gay like his dad did. I believe that having a relationship with God and committing oneself to participate in the community of God's people are more important than whether one is gay or not. He asked how I feel. I told him how I feel. Nothing dishonest about that.

What about [Matthew 6:10]? I am a part of the Kingdom of God, but I'm in this world. So how can you say that the Kingdom of God is not of this world? The ancient Israelite theocracy pleased God at times. In fact, there were periods when they were quite successful in doing God's will.

When I read the OT, the pattern that I notice is that when the leadership/government fails to uphold Godly values, the people stray from God's ways. But when the governors are Godly, the people follow God's ways. I would say rules/government have a major effect on people's hearts.

It's not idolatrous to have human leadership. God appointed several judges over a nation. They were given the authority they needed to rule the people as well that the tools (e.g. wisdom, kindness, patience) they needed to avoid abusing their authority.

I believe it's something like this:

**[Person A]:** Hey, are you on my side or their side?

**[Person B]:** I'm on God's side. And I'm the leader of everyone on God's side.

**[Person A]:** Oh ok. Well I definitely want to be on God's side. I'll do whatever you say.

I've heard lots of sermons where the main point is, "You should be asking God what he wants you to do - not telling God what you want him to do," and they try to come up with so many examples and analogies. I always wonder why they don't just use this story. It's directly applicable to daily life.

> There's a difference between living in the world and trying to create a worldly government of the organized Christian religion, with, presumably, the enforcement of religious laws and morals on all citizens, even non-Christians.

But the kingdom of God only enforced its values on the people of God, including non-members who had joined the community. But everyone else was considered an outsider and treated as such. Godly practices were not expected of outsiders.

> The Israelite theocracy failed, time and again.

But every time the Israelites ran into trouble, it was because they had strayed from the system that God set up. The system worked as long as the people followed it. The theocracy was a major success as long as it was followed.

I think everyone could benefit from the model of a good community. Admittedly, there are many religious institutions that don't set a very good example. But I'm talking about the ones that do it right.

Growing up in a religious setting has been beneficial to me in countless ways, but one really big one has been realizing the power of a community in which people love and support one another despite their vastly different backgrounds, circumstances, and perspectives. It's incredible to see how a group of people, who would otherwise probably never be in the same room together, can be drawn together by their common understanding that happiness comes from serving others and their common goal of pursuing that which they believe to be good and pure. Moreover, the community is made up of a broad cross section of society, so it contains all kinds of skills and disciplines. Because of this, the community is capable of achieving great things, even with few resources, and while maintaining a humble attitude.

Of course all of that I've described is not unique to any specific group. This is how an ancient community was designed to function long before a central religious figure. What that figure brought was a reminder that this community was not meant to be exclusive. He taught that the community of believers should have an open-door policy for anyone who wanted to be a part of it (by both contributing and benefiting). I think the only thing that could be better than such a unified community is allowing others to join it.

It makes me so sad that there are entire institutions that don't understand this; they're missing the point completely. Then outsiders wonder why anyone would want to be a part of that. I wish everyone could experience it the way I have.

No. It's not critical to understand everything about the nature of a supreme being. For instance, we could debate for a very long time about the shape and color of a supreme being. One could argue that those attributes are part of a supreme being's nature and therefore we should know them and believe in them. But most people don't waste their time with such trivial topics, because in the end it makes no difference what color or shape a supreme being is. So simply saying that something is part of a supreme being's nature does not give it some inherent importance. Similarly, I'm asking what makes the Trinitarian understanding of a supreme being important? What difference does it make?

Of course you have to know **something** about them. You have to know many things about them. But there are also many things that you don't need to know. There are lots of trivial attributes of my nature (like the way some of the freckles on my arm almost form a straight line) that my spouse does not need to know in order for us to maintain a good relationship. So what makes the Trinitarian understanding of God one of the important things and not one of the trivial things?
The Gospel of John explicitly presents Jesus as divine, particularly in its opening verses which identify him as the Word who was with God and was God.
"If only you would be altogether silent! For you, that would be wisdom." -The Divine to Job (Job 13:5)

Followers of the divine were well-acquainted with divine forgiveness long before the central figure's death (Nehemiah 9:17, Matthew 6:12). And regardless of the central figure's divinity, he lived a perfect life and died a sinner's death, which is a sufficient sacrifice. So it seems like the gospel is still good news even if the central figure wasn't divine.

You stated that the aspect of the gospel necessitating the figure's divinity is the concept of self-sacrifice. I was highlighting that the divine nature is characterized by love and forgiveness regardless of whether that figure was divine or engaged in self-sacrifice.
Those are marvelous things if they are true. But even if they aren't isn't he amazing and loving?

If you read the post, you'll see that that is exactly the reason that climate change should be a priority. Wealthy individuals are least susceptible to the effects of climate change. But the poor and marginalized are the ones dying from it (in droves). It would be hypocritical for religious adherents to pretend they care for others by "spreading the gospel and witnessing to others," while simultaneously hurting the same people.

We know that natural disasters are caused (at least in part) by factors that are within our control. For example, the Dust Bowl of the 1930s was a series of three "natural disasters" (drought and dust storms) that were caused by [farmers failing to use dryland farming methods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_Bowl). The solution was to educate farmers on the proper way to farm on the great plains, and we haven't had a dust bowl since. The current climate change problem is the same thing but in a larger geographic area and over a longer time scale.
Yeah, but I couldn't come up with a wording that I liked. I figured people would know what I mean.
I would love to know why. Which of the points do you disagree with?

They differ in that one is physical and the other is metaphysical. If you're willing to accept that difference and compare them accordingly, then I think it's fair to say that the two are similar. If you doubt the metaphysical altogether, then this conversation would have to be very long.

If humans are causing the problem, then what makes you think it's too big for humans to fix? As pointed out in the post, humans were made the stewards of the world and its inhabitants.

> Before the earth goes beyond the tipping point and life on earth is threatened

As mentioned in the post, many thousands have already died and are dying still.

> Instead of getting involved in the world

Of all the wisdom in scripture, none advocates for complacency. We are obligated to help the less fortunate, even when we played no role in their affliction. How much more when we are the source of their suffering!

I see. To an extent, I agree with you. I was careful not to say that climate change should be anyone's **highest** priority. For example, stopping violent crime is something that requires a direct as well as indirect approach, and the direct approach may not always be resource-efficient. Same with caring for those in desperate need.

However, as the post points out, almost all of the actions that we can take to help the planet don't require the expenditure of resources. In fact, most of them will actually reduce expenses, which will free up resources for helping people more directly.

I can't think of a situation in which the religious organization's efforts to help people would prevent it from also helping the planet.
That's kinda the point of the original post. It first lays out the evidence. Then it explains the conclusions that are drawn from the evidence.

That sounds like a lot of excuses to not try. I don't know the effects of everyone changing their habits for the better, though it's hard for me to imagine any realistic negative consequences. However, I have examined my own life and noted every possible way for me to reduce my own carbon footprint, and I have begun to do so. And I expect others to do the same.
What do you take that verse to mean and how is it relevant?
By what definition of religion? I do not worship it and it does not take away from my worship of God. In fact, I take care of the planet as an act of service to God.
I hope that if/when we implement some semblance of a solution to climate change, we will return to solve the root problem, which is this kind of thinking.

I think a religious figure attempted to address this in the parable where a man leaves his servants in charge. He expects that when he returns he will find that his servants are working and have been working in his absence. The servants shouldn't just sit around waiting for the master.

This is a really good question and I'm disappointed that it to so long for someone to ask it. When any person suggests that others should change their actions, that person should be asked to give an account of his/her own actions. Fewer people would tell others what to do if they knew they would be held to the same standard.

My spouse and I were typical suburban American consumers. I am proud to say that when we realized we were part of the problem, we radically redesigned our lifestyle and left consumerism behind. The only way I could share this post was knowing that I'm not asking anyone to do anything that I haven't done myself.

But I'm not the political left. So are my concerns legitimate or do you think I also have an agenda?

What is the political left's agenda? Getting all the scientists in the world to accept climate change and make up evidence to support it seems like a huge gamble and an ineffective way to push an agenda.

You're right that the problem requires cooperation, but the first step is making personal changes. This is true for anyone trying to get someone else to take some action. You must first be an example. Then people are more likely to cooperate.

My detailed assessment in the original post does not use any politically motivated sources. The information is peer-reviewed and factual - not opinions.

I have done my best to fairly examine both political perspectives and it seems that both sides potentially have something to gain. Yes, some people use this issue purely for political gain, just like some people abuse their positions in religious institutions for selfish gain. You must look past that and assess the truth of the matter despite the human selfishness surrounding it.

There are three reasons.

1. I don't think the civil rights leader was wicked or deceptive. At worst, he was undecided.

2. Of the reasons that the religious figure gave to despair or be angry, hell wasn't one. He directed his followers' attention toward their neighbor's wellbeing in this life - not their own wellbeing in the afterlife.

3. If anyone is in hell, it's not because someone else caused them to go there. It's no one's fault but their own.

For the sake of promoting discussion:

1. Isn't that what deacons are for? If not deacons, then close friends?

2. You could say the same for musicians, but religious organizations often have plenty of them, or they go out of their way to find them. Obviously, some congregations would have trouble implementing this immediately, but if the religious organization promoted learning useful skills in the same way as music, then I don't see why they would have trouble finding skilled labor among the members.

3. It would probably help to have an organizer. But if that organizer delegates to responsible people, he/she shouldn't have to commit much time to managing them. Even if it did take a lot of time, it doesn't have to be the same person all the time does it?

4. Why?

5. Often times the religious organization/staff is honest with its funds and there's no reason to doubt them. However, part of being equally yoked and bearing one another's burdens means I pick up the slack when my neighbor falls short, even if it's my neighbor's fault. Even if it's the fault of the doubter, I'm suggesting that the religious organization could help by using donations to feed and clothe those in desperate need rather than pocket some of it.

6. Are you suggesting that it would be a lower quality ministry if responsibilities were shared or if it required less time?

Thank you.

I understand that you're interpreting this verse to mean money instead of honor, but why do you think that? In an honor-shame society, it's reasonable to think that honor here actually means honor.
But isn't everyone in the religious organization expected to serve? Why not pay everyone?
That's a good distinction to make, but in your analogy, the flock is made of people who are also expected to serve, so shouldn't they all be paid?

I wasn't trying to generalize. I understood your explanation to be this:

*The clergy member works by serving the congregation, so he should be paid.*

Did I misunderstand?

I'm wondering why that can't apply to everyone who serves? Or, why can't his work be distributed so that anyone could do it in their free time, thus freeing the money up to help people in more desperate circumstances?
At my current religious institution, the divine presence is acknowledged (not being facetious) and it seems to work pretty well.

It seems that you have missed the point of the post. I know that some people have chosen to serve the religious organization in lieu of secular work, and they expect to be paid. What I'm saying is that that draws a lot of unnecessary negative attention, and it seems like we could avoid that if we would just divide the work load of service so **everybody** in the religious organization (including leadership) is free to earn their own money instead of taking their income from the donations.

What is the benefit? In what case would it be preferable to have one person do the work of the whole congregation (and pay him) instead of having the whole congregation do the work (and use the money to help the needy)?

> should have the same salary regardless

Yes, but that salary is usually funded by the donations of the religious organization as I said.

> if you expect to have a full time pastor

As I said in the original post, couldn't the workload be divided so that you don't need a full time religious leader?

I understand that in some parts of the world, most people lack the education or time to sufficiently teach or help with leading. In that case, maybe they can delegate one person to get the education and commit the time while everyone else pays to put food on his table. The early church leaders would be an example of that extreme situation.

However, as you mentioned, that's not ideal. And if it's not ideal, then we should avoid it if possible, right? In most of the developed world today, it seems perfectly possible. In the US for instance, most people are educated and have some amount of free time. So why not have everyone pitch in to do the work instead of paying one person to do it?

I gave two possible ways in the original post:

1. Distribute the workload so that nobody has to serve full time. That would allow everyone a chance to earn their own income.

2. People could work hard and spend their money wisely to build up their savings before going into ministry so that they could afford to work for free.

Also, attending a theological school is not the only way to get an education or to effectively lead a congregation. Also, people do not have to take on debt to go to a theological school.

> If they are doing work then they deserve to be paid.

...unless you're a layperson? As a layperson, I am expected to serve my community while earning my own income, and I am not paid for it. So why pay some people and not others? Is there something fundamentally different between the work that I do and the work that my pastor or music leader does?

> That's unrealistic

There are a lot of people over at /r/financialindependence who would disagree. My wife and I are on schedule to reach financial independence by age 32 on meager salaries. It's really not that hard if you loosen your hold on material pleasure.

> How many people do you know

I currently know six people who have achieved financial independence before going into ministry so that they could serve without pay.

The things you mentioned seem like reasonable expenses. Of course every necessary expense for the organization to fulfill its role is justified. By "pocket" I meant the portion that goes directly to an individual for some service that is optional (or could be shared by several people so as not to require compensation).

Because the role of a full-time religious leader is not explained in scripture, the term "full-time pastor" has no concrete meaning to me. As I've seen it practiced, it usually means a person who leads the church (at least in Baptist churches where they don't have elders). They prepare at least one sermon per week and maybe a bible study. They are on call day and night to counsel members of the congregation. They manage many of the administrative tasks of the building (if the church has a building). They serve the community. They organize church meetings outside of the Sunday gathering. They are also usually expected to have a seminary background, even though that's not the only way to gain an education and that is not required by scripture.

Meanwhile, many unpaid members of the congregation work full-time jobs in addition to serving the community, leading parts of the congregation, and studying scripture/doctrine/theology. Meanwhile, many other members of the church spend their evenings eating at restaurants, watching television, and doing other unproductive things.

My point is that many of the laity are doing much of the pastor's work for free and many more of the laity are available to do the same.

> You seemed to imply that more funds leads to a higher salary.

I was not implying that. I was simply saying that the pastor is dependent on a constant stream of donations to keep food on his table.

No. I just gave that as one example of the potential drawbacks of having paid staff. There are potentially many others, and I'm not sure I could name the primary one.

What prompted this post are a few realizations that I've had over the last couple of years:

1. Reaching financial independence at a young age is quite feasible for anyone in a developed country.

2. The modern proliferation of information means that many more people can gain a religious education by personal study and mentorship outside of seminary.

3. Many of the laity do less work for the kingdom because they believe that by funding the church, they have done their job.

4. Many nonbelievers would love to be part of a loving, serving community but they aren't open to the church because of money (either rumors or past experiences or suspicion or realistic concerns).

5. I have had the opportunity to participate in a church that has no paid pastors or staff and there has been a long list of tremendous benefits.

6. Some paid pastors live in bigger houses than I can afford.

7. Some paid pastors have really bad personal finance skills.

> If your religious leader has no training...sounds like a shifty religious leader.

You seem to be assuming that the only way to be a good counselor or leader or to have sound theological understanding is through formal training. A godly community should naturally produce many good leaders and wise, learned counselors. I think that's the point of, "Impress them on your children. Talk about them when sit at home and when you walk along the road..."

It's nice that your religious teacher does all of those things and I'm not saying he shouldn't. My question is, how do you justify paying him to do those things? Is there no possible alternative? Perhaps:

- eliminating the tasks that are not necessary?
- delegating the tasks to those with free time even if that means training and ordaining more people?
- scheduling a time for questions instead of allowing for the luxury of spontaneity?
- have the laity spend less time studying and more time serving the community, thus requiring less preparation time?

These are just some ideas. They are not exhaustive and they may not be feasible right now. I'm just trying to propose another (possibly better) way for the future.

> You do not appreciate the time it takes to be a proper community leader

I am a proper community leader, and I am not paid for it. I also work a full-time secular job. I hear the excuse that it takes too much time, and would like to know what exactly requires a single person to commit so much time and energy that he/she cannot possibly work for money like everyone else.

My spouse and I joined last year, but I believe the congregation has been operating for about eight years. We meet in a very small venue, so when the group grows larger than about 40 people, we have to split into separate meetings, so I'm not sure how many people there are total, but I know they have had to split several times. The group I meet with currently has about 16 people. Being so small, it's a very familial community.

> If you don't have someone calling the shots

What shots? It's organized so that there is never an opportunity for someone to make a unilateral decision. We pray and study together to collectively decide what actions we should take as a community and we take turns volunteering to organize activities as we are available.

> you will soon

What makes you so sure? Is it really that hard to believe that a group of mature, faithful people is not dependent on a single paid leader in order to follow God's will?

When your goals are clearly defined, it's usually pretty easy to determine what expenses are necessary to fulfill them. I agree that that will vary as the needs of each community are different.

I also agree that it is not bad (it's great) if someone is able to commit all of their time to serving. In fact, that's my goal when I retire in a few years. The question here is how you justify paying a person who **chose** not to earn money in the usual way when that money could be used to help the needy instead.

> It's not impossible

That's the theme, that I'm seeing throughout this thread. It's not impossible to have unpaid staff - it's just harder.

I agree that the usual responsibilities of the religious leader are things that must be done. But scripture does not require or even recommend that those jobs be done by just one person or a small group of people. In the early church, very few people had the information they needed to fill those roles, so yeah their burden was heavier than their congregations'.

If people are getting lost in the community, there must be a better solution than taking money that could be used to feed/clothe the needy to hire a "shepherd." Perhaps splitting into smaller groups?

> one of them is to support those teaching the word

Again, it was practical necessity for the early church. That's simply not the case now. Now it's optional.

I don't see how those other topics relate to this one. 

As for asking my religious leader, I currently attend a congregation with no paid staff, so the answer from there is, "It's unnecessary and an unwise use of resources."
Save your money before spending it. That's the secret formula for avoiding all debt.

The difference between this situation and that one is spending one's own money versus spending someone else's donated money.

I don't treat all money with that same high regard - just donated money. People give their money to the religious organization expecting it to be spent responsibly. The organization therefore has an obligation to not only spend it responsibly, but to spend it as responsibly as they possibly can.

I guess I do have a fairly low regard for the expectation to be paid for something that almost everyone else does for free. I understand that it would be an added challenge for leaders to earn their money outside the organization, but perhaps leading is supposed to be more difficult than following. Or perhaps the leaders should be able to rely on help from their followers.

I have already made the case that it's different today than it was then. It comes down to the economy, and the economies in developed countries today are extremely different from the economy of Judea in the first century.

> why not a more democratic structure

That is one solution that I proposed - if we pay one person because he/she is loaded with responsibilities, then couldn't we distribute those responsibilities and eliminate  his/her need for compensation? The other solution I proposed would be to keep the same structure and simply not pay the staff. This would cause a subsequent shift where only those who work hardest, spend their money most wisely, save most responsibly, and want to lead for leadership's sake alone (rather than income) would be put in a position of leadership.

I would say that the first solution lowers the bar for leadership, while the second solution raises it.

A third solution might be a combination of the second solution with a slight alteration of the structure so that staff serve only temporarily so that they don't have to achieve full financial independence. They could go back to work after serving full time.

And these are just my ideas, I'm sure that as situations vary, people could be more creative than me in coming up with alternatives to paying clergy.

> would be difficult to replicate without dedicated people

I understand that it is always difficult to transition to a new way of doing things, but it's not impossible. And the fact that something is difficult shouldn't even make us hesitate.

> that's where the elder role is important

Perhaps, but some might say that's where the diversity of the congregation is important. I've been counseled by elders, and that's good, but I've also been counseled by church members who have been though similar trials and that is just as good if not better.

The poor stewardship of money is, again just one example that I gave of the potential drawbacks of paying clergy. Another potential drawback is highlighted in your example. If I pay someone to fix my plumbing, the assumption is that they do it so that I don't have to. But paying a pastor is not the same because, even though I pay my tithe to support him, I am still obligated to serve. Many church members believe that by giving donations their job is done. Jesus's teachings did not allow for anyone to hire out the work of the church. The obligation rests on each member.

I meant that (except in special circumstances such as disability) one could work to earn money until one has saved up enough to go to school without taking on debt. The same applies to paying for cars or anything else.
Which principles? That church leadership should be paid? Or that earning money from secular work is the high road?

The role of an elder is not defined in scripture, though Paul does say that elders should be righteous. Pastors aren't mentioned at all.

So I don't think pastors or elders have absolute roles. I could tell you the ways I've seen those roles practiced, but I don't think that's what you're asking.

I think a church body should be structured like a mustard bush. Each part has its own job. While some jobs are more central (you might call them elders) and some are out-reaching, they are all critical to the function of the bush, which is to create more bushes before it's season is finished. The parts are not supported by or organized around a solid trunk, nor do they support a trunk. Rather, all parts are tightly interwoven, supporting each other. It should not be monolithic and powerful so as not to promote corruption as there would be nothing to gain. And it should not outlive its usefulness. Mustard plants are annuals. That is, once they've accomplished their purpose, they die. Churches should be purpose-built to establish and promote the next generation of Christ followers, and when they have done their job, they should be allowed to dissolve, or at least transform into the next thing. When you have full-time ministers who are dependent on a constant stream of donations to keep food on their plates, they can be easily distracted from the church's mission, forcing it to overstay its usefulness.

I have to say I definitely did not expect someone to say that here. I'm impressed that you not only believe that, but that you are acting on it. I too hope to plant a church in the next 5-10 years with the same principles. I believe that a lot of disaffected Christians and nonbelievers will find the structure you described refreshing and welcome.

Yes, that is a valid alternative. But you asked me how to avoid debt so I told you. Also, by taking on debt, you have some major disadvantages:

- It costs you a lot more money in the long run because of interest and fees.

- You're debt/income ratio is higher, which means any other loans will require a higher down payment or higher interest rate, again costing you more money in the long run. Or you might not even qualify.

- You risk not getting a job after graduation in which case you can't pay off the loan, so you hurt your credit and the interest grows. Again, costing you more money in the long run. Or you have to get a secular job, just like I suggested except this way you accumulate interest.

- You are dependent on a constant stream of income which could put you in a tight spot if God's calling turns out not to be very profitable (e.g. homeless ministry).

- You will require a higher salary from the church than you would otherwise. That is, you will be a greater burden on the church than you would be if you had just saved up your money.

- Because your income will be provided by the church, all of these added costs will ultimately be paid by whatever church you end up serving. Though at that point, it seems like they're serving you.

All of this perpetuates the need to pay the church staff, a problem that I pointed out in the original post.

> like everyone else

Yes, many people do this with school, cars, houses, boats, RVs, etc. It's popular, but it's not smart. And it's not right to pass on the added costs to faithful donors.
I think this is pretty well demonstrated by people calling their dogs their children, as if the only difference is the fur. Your human child is not just a pet for your pleasure. He/she is a person.
I would love to meet my descendant. I love learning about my family history, but it would be so much cooler to know my family's future.

No, a hypocrite is someone who conceals his/her wrongdoing - a subtle but important distinction for this discussion. Nonetheless, I agree that members of a specific religious group should not be hypocritical.

The sacred text teaches that members of this group are called to repent from sin and become a holy (set apart in purity) and perfect (meaning fully grown, not flawless) people. For these members to tell the world that we are no different from the world would be contrary to the organization's purpose. If we cannot offer a community that is freedom from hatred, greed and all the other worldly things, then what are we inviting people into?
I came here to say exactly this. Life after death is uncompelling and largely speculative. Generally, a witness' job is not to speculate, but to speak to what they know of the past and the present.

You're exactly right. A religious figure taught a lot of very valuable lessons, but "don't go to hell" was neither the moral of any of the lessons nor the theme of his ministry. If we're to follow his example, hell (whatever it may be) is not for us to worry about.

This is the only comment here that's actually based on scripture. In the Bible, Heaven is the dwelling place of God and angels, and certain very special people are said to have gone there. The belief that Jesus allows us to go there is a later formulation. It's not clear which (if any) references to hell are meant to be taken literally.
